paras: Stay in your seat after any live show and watch the credits. Most people leave before the names start, and that is a pity, because the credits are the only place where the whole machine is visible. The host is the person who everybody remembers. The credits are a list of the people who made the host possible: the stage manager who counted the seconds, the engineer who kept the vocals clean, the runner who found the missing cable at five past eight. Almost all of the work that makes a show feel easy happens behind the scenes, and almost all of it goes unnoticed.

Every production has a go-to person, and it is rarely the one with the biggest title. It is the person who knows which door is locked, which microphone is unreliable, and which producer needs to hear bad news first. When something goes wrong, people do not look at the organization chart. They look for the one person that they trust to fix it. If that person is sick on a Thursday, somebody has to step in, and the whole team discovers in about ten minutes how much it depended on a single name.

The weakest point in a production is usually not a person. It is a handoff: the moment when a piece of work passes from the team that made it to the team that needs it. The arrangement which was perfect on Monday arrives on Wednesday without the notes that explained it. The best teams solve this with one simple rule. Every task has a point of contact, a single person who answers questions about it, and that person keeps everybody else in the loop. It sounds bureaucratic. It is the opposite: it is the reason nobody has to guess.

There is a lesson here for anybody who wants to run a project one day. You cannot do everything, so you have to delegate, and delegating well means knowing who does what, not only what needs to be done. Before a big decision, list the stakeholders, the people who will live with the result, and talk to them first. And when the show is over, thank the unsung ones by name. The credits roll for a reason. Somebody should read them.

choices: To argue that the host of a show gets too much attention.
To show that a production depends on people nobody sees, and how good teams organize around them.
To explain how to write the credits for a television show.

items.situation: Describe your go-to person at work, using who.
tips: She is the person who fixes the in-ear mixes before anybody asks.
Who for people. The clause tells you which person.

items.situation: Describe a place that matters in your week, using where.
tips: The control room is the place where every decision gets made.
Where for places: where plus a full sentence, with no extra in at the end.

items.situation: Describe a piece of equipment you depend on, using which.
tips: The console which we use for the live week is ten years old.
Which for things. That works too, and it is more informal.

items.situation: Now say the same kind of sentence with that, about a person.
tips: The runner that I trust most is on vacation this week.
That works for people and things in everyday speech.

items.situation: Say who the point of contact is for something in your project.
tips: Dara is the point of contact who answers questions about the backing tracks.
One person, one task, one clause that says so.

items.situation: Thank somebody whose work goes unnoticed, in one sentence.
tips: I want to thank the engineer who kept the vocals clean all season.
Name the person, then say exactly what they did.

listenings.text: I have been a stage manager for eleven years, and for most of that time I was the person who stands behind the curtain with a headset and a stopwatch. Nobody in the audience knows my name, and that is exactly how it should be. But here is something that took me years to understand. Every show has a go-to person who is not on the call sheet as anything special. On our show it was a sound assistant called Marcos. He was the one who knew which microphone had a weak cable, which singer needed water before every take, and which door to the stage got stuck in the rain. One Thursday he was sick, and somebody else had to step in. The show still happened. But in about ten minutes, all of us discovered how much of the evening had been sitting quietly on one person. The next week, we wrote down everything that Marcos knew. It took four pages.

When I started as a music director, I thought the hard part would be the music. It was not. The hard part was the handoffs: the arrangement which leaves my desk on Monday and arrives at the band on Wednesday, the click track that goes to the video team, the lyric sheet that goes to the captions. Every one of those is a place where something can get lost. So we made one rule, and it changed everything. Every file has a point of contact, one person who answers questions about it, and that person keeps the others in the loop. It sounds like paperwork, and it is the opposite. Before the rule, people guessed. After the rule, people asked. And I learned to delegate properly for the first time, because I finally knew who was doing what, not only what needed to be done.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says that the host is the person who everybody remembers. He explains that the people who make the show possible work behind the scenes. He says that their go-to person is a sound assistant who knows every cable. He adds that the weakest point is the handoff, the moment when work passes to the next team. He says that every file now has a point of contact who keeps everybody in the loop. Then he thanks the people whose work usually goes unnoticed.
